network.reasoning:
Right at the start, 39.15 dBm transmission power is a red flag. That's a standard full-power output for UE. If a device is near the gNB, it wouldn't need to run at full power - it would naturally use lower power to maintain a connection without wasting energy or causing interference. So high transmit power suggests the UE is having to work harder to maintain a link.

Looking at the RSRP of -117.3 dBm (mean), that's definitely on the lower side of acceptable signal strength. RSRP ranges from -44 dBm (excellent) to about -130 dBm (marginally usable). -117 dBm is in the weak signal range, although it's stable - not fluctuating wildly. Stable weak signal is different from intermittent or poor signal. This is consistent with an outer cell edge location rather than an indoor or obstructed environment where signal would be more unstable.

The MCS is another key indicator. DL MCS of 7 is quite low - the MCS scale goes from 0 (very low rate, low reliability) to about 28 (high rate, high reliability). So a DL MCS of 7 indicates that the UE is receiving data at a low rate due to poor channel conditions. The UL MCS of 14.7 is better but still not optimal, suggesting the UE can transmit somewhat better than it can receive, but both directions show suboptimal performance for a close-in UE.

The BLER is quite telling. The DL BLER is very low (0.00041 mean), which means the downlink has very few transmission errors, which makes sense if the gNB is transmitting at high power and using good channels. But the UL BLER is much higher (0.1 mean), meaning the UE is having significant difficulty transmitting back to the gNB. High UL BLER is a strong indicator of a UE being in a poor location relative to the gNB.

The PRB utilization shows the gNB is trying to schedule more resources for downlink when needed (spikes to ~45 PRBs/43% utilization), but the UE's uplink utilization is very low (mean of 0.96 PRBs). This asymmetry suggests the UE is receiving data but struggling to transmit it back reliably.

The uplink buffer size is also notable, with a high mean of 168.3 KB and peaks up to 1196.3 KB. This indicates the UE has a lot of data to send but can't send it quickly enough due to poor channel conditions. This accumulation of data in the buffer is causing significant delays in transmission.

The traffic pattern is very bursty, with TX_Bytes spiking up to 258,698 Bytes and UL packet counts going up to 66. This burstiness is likely due to the UE having to retransmit data because of errors, and also because it's trying to send large amounts of data that have been queued up in the buffer. The bursty nature of traffic is different from the smooth, continuous traffic seen in good signal conditions.

The fact that TCP is almost entirely used (99.22% DL, 100% UL) is also significant. TCP is a reliable protocol that handles congestion and lost packets, which makes it well-suited for poor channel conditions where packet loss is likely. In good signal conditions, UDP would be more commonly used for things like streaming media where some packet loss is acceptable.

Putting all these indicators together - the UE is using full transmit power, has weak but stable RSRP, low MCS for both directions (though better UL), extremely high UL BLER, low UL PRB utilization, high buffer sizes with data queuing, bursty traffic patterns, and relying almost entirely on TCP - this is the classic signature of a UE located far from the gNB, at the edge of the cell. The UE is in a location where it needs to work hard to maintain the connection and has significant difficulty transmitting data back to the gNB. The signal is weak enough that the UE has to compensate with full power and the gNB has to schedule more resources, but the channel conditions are still poor enough to result in significant errors and retransmissions.

The high variability in traffic volume and packet counts on both the uplink and downlink, especially given the predominant use of TCP, suggests potential issues with congestion, retransmission delays, or other factors affecting network performance.
